subject: Banking
title: Commercial vs Investment Banks
description: A micro-lesson that makes Commercial vs Investment Banks usable.

hook.text: Your local bank takes deposits and makes loans. An investment bank does neither. It deals in companies, not customers.

buildup.text: Commercial banks earn from the spread between deposit interest and loan interest. Investment banks earn from deal fees.

discovery.text: Investment banks help companies raise money, go public, merge with rivals, or sell divisions. Every service earns a fee.

twist.text: After Glass-Steagall was repealed in 1999, the line blurred.

climax.text: One business manufactures credit for households; the other packages capital and advice for corporations.

punchline.text: Your bank serves people. Investment banks serve corporations.

quiz.question: How do investment banks primarily earn revenue?
options: Fees from corporate deals like IPOs and mergers

details.summary: Commercial banks take deposits and make loans to individuals and businesses, while investment banks help companies raise capital, advise on mergers, and trade securities. Glass-Steagall once separated them; today most large banks do both.
details.whyItMatters: The blurring of commercial and investment banking created the too-big-to-fail institutions at the center of the 2008 financial crisis. Understanding the distinction reveals ongoing tensions between risk-taking and deposit safety.
takeaways: Commercial banks earn money from the spread between deposit and loan rates
Investment banks earn fees from advisory, underwriting, and trading
Glass-Steagall separated them from 1933 until its repeal in 1999

faq.question: Why was Glass-Steagall repealed?
faq.answer: Banks lobbied for decades to compete with each other. By the 1990s, regulators had already allowed exceptions. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act formally repealed the separation, allowing banks like Citigroup to combine all financial activities.

faq.question: Did repealing Glass-Steagall cause the 2008 crisis?
faq.answer: Partially. It allowed banks to combine risky trading with deposit-backed lending, creating interconnected institutions whose failure threatened the entire system. However, many factors beyond the repeal contributed to the crisis.
